script.voiceText: [deep, cinematic documentary narrator, calm authority, crisp pace] Try tickling yourself. Right now... [playful, curious, quick] Nothing, right? Every time you move, your brain sends a copy of the command. And scientists think your cerebellum uses that copy to predict exactly what the touch will feel like. Predicted touch? It gets turned DOWN. But a stranger's fingers? No prediction... full sensation. That's why someone else can tickle you... and you can't. In one experiment, a robot delayed people's own touch by a fraction of a second... and it started to feel more ticklish! Your brain isn't just feeling the world. It's PREDICTING it.

claims.claim: Self-produced touch feels less ticklish than the same touch applied externally; the brain's response is reduced.
claims.source: Blakemore, Wolpert & Frith (1998), Central cancellation of self-produced tickle sensation, Nature Neuroscience 1(7):635-640 (fMRI: less somatosensory activity for self-produced touch)

claims.claim: The brain uses a copy of the motor command to predict the sensory result; the cerebellum is thought to make this prediction (hedged: 'scientists think').
claims.source: Blakemore, Wolpert & Frith (1998), as above, which proposes the cerebellum predicts sensory consequences of movement; Kilteni & Ehrsson review frames the cerebellum as the likely source of forward-model predictions

claims.claim: A robot that delayed people's own touch by a fraction of a second made it feel more ticklish.
claims.source: Blakemore, Frith & Wolpert (1999), Spatio-temporal prediction modulates the perception of self-produced stimuli, Journal of Cognitive Neuroscience 11(5):551-559 (tickliness rose with delays up to 200-300 ms)

claims.claim: Someone else can tickle you but you can't: externally produced touch is perceived as more ticklish than self-produced.

storyboard.narration: And scientists think your cerebellum uses that copy to predict exactly what the touch will feel like.

Deep navy background, cool rim light, subtle cyan accents, cinematic documentary realism, shallow depth of field, no text, no letters, no watermark.
storyboard.label: CEREBELLUM · ILLUSTRATIVE
storyboard.motion: Slow orbit around the cerebellum while points of cyan light ripple across its folds.

storyboard.narration: Predicted touch? It gets turned DOWN.
storyboard.visual: Mascot next to a big cartoon volume dial labelled TOUCH; the needle swings from high to low; mascot shrugs.
storyboard.label: PREDICTION

storyboard.narration: But a stranger's fingers? No prediction... full sensation.
storyboard.visual: Photorealistic cinematic close-up, vertical 9:16: another person's fingertips lightly touching the inside of a forearm, the skin catching a warm glow where they touch, goosebumps visible. Deep navy background, cool rim light, subtle cyan accents, cinematic documentary realism, shallow depth of field, no text, no letters, no watermark.
storyboard.label: SOMATOSENSORY RESPONSE
storyboard.motion: The fingertips trail slowly along the forearm; tiny goosebumps rise. Slow, gentle.

storyboard.narration: That's why someone else can tickle you... and you can't.
storyboard.visual: Two mascots: one tickles the other, who laughs helplessly; then the laughing mascot tries to tickle itself and goes blank.
storyboard.label: SAME TOUCH, DIFFERENT BRAIN

storyboard.narration: In one experiment, a robot delayed people's own touch by a fraction of a second...
storyboard.visual: Photorealistic cinematic lab scene, vertical 9:16: a small precise robotic arm with a soft foam tip touching the open palm of a person's hand resting on a dark lab bench, cyan rim light on the metal. Deep navy background, cool rim light, subtle cyan accents, cinematic documentary realism, shallow depth of field, no text, no letters, no watermark.
storyboard.label: EXPERIMENT · BLAKEMORE ET AL. 1999
storyboard.motion: The robot arm slowly strokes the foam tip across the palm; the fingers twitch slightly.

storyboard.narration: and it started to feel more ticklish!
storyboard.visual: Mascot giggling, squirming; a counter DELAY 0 → 300 ms and a TICKLE meter rising beside it.
storyboard.label: DELAY = SURPRISE

storyboard.narration: Your brain isn't just feeling the world. It's PREDICTING it.
storyboard.visual: Mascot looks up at a glowing cartoon brain that projects a little dotted 'forecast' of a hand touching; mascot smiles knowingly. Then end card.
storyboard.label: THE PREDICTING BRAIN

metadata.title: Why Can't You Tickle Yourself? Your Brain Predicts It #shorts
metadata.description:
Try tickling yourself. Nothing happens, because your brain predicts your own touch and turns it down before you feel it.

Sources:
- Blakemore, Wolpert & Frith (1998), Nature Neuroscience 1:635-640, "Central cancellation of self-produced tickle sensation"
- Blakemore, Frith & Wolpert (1999), Journal of Cognitive Neuroscience 11:551-559, "Spatio-temporal prediction modulates the perception of self-produced stimuli"

Visuals are AI-generated illustrations.
